analysis.one_liner: Ends immigration detention and ankle monitoring, redirecting funds to community services.
analysis.headline: A House bill to abolish immigration detention and electronic monitoring, with 17 Democratic sponsors and no Republican support, sits in two House committees with no action beyond subcommittee referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the release of detained noncitizens on their own recognizance within six months, repeal the core federal statutes authorizing immigration detention and ankle monitoring, terminate government contracts with detention and monitoring companies within two years, and bar federal money from ankle monitors and certain ICE enforcement operations. It would replace that spending with a new grant program funding community nonprofits to provide housing help, mental health care, English classes, job assistance, and immigration legal help. The bill was introduced in January 2026 and referred to the House Judiciary and Homeland Security Committees, which control whether it ever gets a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Noncitizens currently in immigration detention or on electronic ankle monitors would be released from custody and surveillance. Immigrant families and communities affected by immigration enforcement would gain access to voluntary housing, health, legal, and employment services. Community-based nonprofits would gain a new funding stream to deliver those services.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Department of Homeland Security to release any noncitizen it has detained on their own recognizance within six months of enactment [S2].

Repeals the federal statutes authorizing immigration detention and mandatory detention, and terminates all federal contracts with detention and monitoring facilities within two years, after which no federal funds may go to detention or monitoring programs [S2].
Requires removal of all ankle monitors from noncitizens within six months and bans federal spending on ankle monitoring programs [S2].

Creates a grant program through the Department of Health and Human Services funding community nonprofits — barred from any law-enforcement role — to provide housing, mental health, healthcare, employment, English classes, education, and immigration legal services, with services voluntary and free of surveillance [S2].

Bars ICE 'Operations and Support' funds from being used for civil immigration arrests, detention, or removals, and ends federal funding for information-sharing partnerships with state and local police to identify noncitizens for immigration enforcement [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Private prison and detention companies and electronic monitoring vendors would lose their federal contracts and revenue. Taxpayers would fund the new services grant program, with money redirected away from detention and enforcement operations. Federal, state, and local agencies would lose the ability to detain noncitizens or share immigration-status information with federal authorities.
analysis.who_pays_short: Detention and monitoring contractors, ICE operations

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates all immigration detention authority, including for noncitizens facing removal who may have serious criminal records, releasing them instead on their own recognizance — an honest supporter must acknowledge this removes any custody option [S2].

It repeals the grounds of deportability for public charge and unlawful voting, and bars state and local police from communicating immigration-status information to federal agencies, which critics would call a major pullback in immigration enforcement [S2].

Ending ICE civil enforcement funding and detention contracts within two years would require a large reorganization of the immigration enforcement system, with transition costs for agencies and communities [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits fall on a group with little political power — people in detention and under electronic surveillance — while the costs fall on a well-funded detention and monitoring industry and on agencies that lose enforcement tools. The main honest objection is the total elimination of any detention authority, including for people facing removal; a narrower bill preserving custody for specific categories would be easier to defend. As written, it is a maximal rewrite of the enforcement system.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary and Homeland Security Committees, which sent pieces of it to subcommittees; nothing has happened since.

narrative.text: Rep. Delia Ramirez introduced the bill on January 21, 2026, joined by original cosponsors including Reps. Clarke, Velazquez, Davis of Illinois, Lee of Pennsylvania, and Tlaib [S2].
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the House Homeland Security Committee on the day of introduction [S1].
The next day, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Immigration Integrity, Security, and Enforcement and the Homeland Security Subcommittee on Border Security and Enforcement [S4].
The bill has 16 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no further action since the subcommittee referrals [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private detention and electronic monitoring companies keep their federal contracts and revenues, since the bill has not advanced. Immigrant communities gained nothing yet, but lost nothing either.

for.name: Rep. Delia Ramirez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to abolish immigration detention and electronic monitoring and redirect funding to community services [S1].

for.name: 16 of 217 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; original cosponsors included Reps. Clarke of New York, Velazquez, Davis of Illinois, Lee of Pennsylvania, and Tlaib [S3].

for.name: Immigrant-rights and abolition advocacy groups
for.what_they_did: Have long campaigned to end immigrant detention and ankle monitoring and to shift funds to community-based services, providing the political base for bills like this one.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling committee schedules and floor action (223 of 435 seats)
against.what_they_did: Controls the House and its committees; took no action to advance the bill beyond referral and gave it no hearing or vote [S4].

against.name: Private prison and electronic monitoring industry
against.what_they_did: Would lose all federal immigration detention and monitoring contracts under the bill; the industry has a record of lobbying and campaign spending to preserve detention funding.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 sponsors are Democrats; Republicans hold 223 of 435 House seats and control the committees that would have to move the bill.

industries.note: Companies that own and operate detention facilities under federal contracts — GEO Group and CoreCivic are the largest — would have those contracts terminated within two years and be barred from future detention work. Their revenue depends directly on the detention system the bill abolishes.

Suppliers of ankle monitors and tracking services, largely the same companies that run detention, would lose all federal monitoring business within six months. Their interest in continued surveillance runs against the people being monitored.

The bill creates a new federal grant stream for nonprofits providing housing, health, legal, and employment services to people affected by immigration enforcement, with a carve-out barring organizations involved in law enforcement. These groups' interest runs alongside the people they would serve.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, no committee action beyond subcommittee referral, and a House majority that has shown no interest in the bill, the realistic path is that it dies at the end of the 119th Congress without a hearing or vote. Similar detention-abolition bills introduced in prior Congresses have never reached the floor.
